summary: Describes using a Service Function Forwarder label, similar to a pseudowire or VPN label, to mark that a Network Service Header sits between an MPLS label stack and the original packet. This lets SFC packets cross an MPLS network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8596 describes how to carry Service Function Chaining packets across a network that uses MPLS. A dedicated label, allocated by the node that will receive the packet, marks the payload as one that carries a Network Service Header, and tells that node which forwarding instance to hand it to.

questions: mpls transport for service function chaining
how do you carry nsh in mpls
how does mpls transport service function chaining
subtitle: Carrying Service Function Chaining packets through an MPLS network with a label of their own.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining packets carry a Network Service Header, and an MPLS transport network needs some way to know that its payload is not an ordinary IP packet, so that it can be delivered to the right forwarding instance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts a Service Function Forwarder Label at the bottom of the MPLS label stack, above the NSH and the original packet, allocates that label from the downstream receiver's own label space, and sets its TTL to 1.
tldr.outcome: From the SFC point of view the encapsulation is equivalent to the other transport encapsulations of the NSH, and it uses well-established MPLS procedures with no new protocol elements and no IANA actions.

facts.value: At the bottom of the label stack, above the NSH

today: RFC 8596 is an Informational document from June 2019 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It adds no protocol elements and allocates no code points, so it describes a way of carrying the NSH over MPLS rather than a standard in its own right.

sections.title: What This Adds to Service Function Chaining
sections.content:
Several transport encapsulations for the Service Function Chaining (SFC) Network Service Header (NSH) already exist, such as Ethernet, UDP and GRE. This document describes an MPLS transport encapsulation for the NSH and how to use a Service Function Forwarder (SFF) Label to indicate the presence of the NSH in the MPLS packet payload. That allows SFC packets using the NSH to be forwarded between SFFs in an MPLS transport network, where MPLS interconnects the network nodes that contain one or more SFFs. The label is also used to select between multiple SFFs in the destination MPLS node.

From the SFC perspective this encapsulation is equivalent to the other transport encapsulations of packets using the NSH. The RFC illustrates this by adding a line to the next-hop SPI and SI-to-network overlay network locator mapping table of RFC 8300: Service Path Identifier 25 and Service Index 220 map to next hop Label 5467 with transport encapsulation MPLS.

SFF Labels are similar to other service labels at the bottom of an MPLS label stack that denote the contents of the MPLS payload as something other than a normally routed IP packet, such as a Layer 2 pseudowire, an IP packet routed in a VPN context with a private address, or an Ethernet virtual private wire service. The document follows well-established MPLS procedures and requires no actions by IANA and no new protocol extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Service Function Chaining sends a packet through a chain of network functions, and the chain travels inside a header called the Network Service Header. If the network underneath is MPLS, the receiving node has to be able to tell that the payload is one of these special packets rather than ordinary IP. This RFC uses an MPLS label to do that.

sections.title: The SFF Label and How It Is Allocated
sections.content:
The encapsulation is a standard MPLS label stack with an SFF Label at the bottom of the stack, followed by an NSH as defined by RFC 8300 and the NSH original packet or frame.

Much like a pseudowire label, an SFF Label MUST be allocated by the downstream receiver of the NSH from its per-platform label space, since the meaning of the label is the same no matter which incoming interface it arrives on. If the receiving node supports more than one SFF, that is, more than one SFC forwarding instance, the SFF Label can select the proper SFF, by having the receiving node advertise more than one SFF Label to its upstream sending nodes as appropriate. How the receiving node advertises those labels is out of scope for this document, and the RFC notes that several methods are possible, such as a protocol exchange, or a controller that manages both ends using NETCONF and YANG, BGP or the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). One BGP-based method has already been defined and is documented separately.

The SFF Label will usually be at the bottom of the label stack, but there may be cases where there are additional label stack entries beneath it. When an Associated Channel Header that applies to the SFF is carried, a Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) will be in the label stack below the SFF. Similarly, an Entropy Label Indicator and Entropy Label may be carried below the SFF in the label stack. This is identical to the situation with VPN labels. The document does not define the setting of the Traffic Class field in the SFF Label.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is allocated by the node that will receive the packet, from the same pool it uses for other labels that mean something other than a normal IP packet, such as pseudowire labels. If a node runs more than one forwarding instance, it can hand out one label per instance and the label alone picks the right one.

sections.title: Building the Label Stack at the Sender
sections.content:
When one SFF sends an SFC packet with an NSH to another SFF over an MPLS transport network, the MPLS node holding the sending SFF builds a label stack that carries the packet to the destination MPLS node holding the receiving SFF. The stack is built in three steps.

First, zero or more labels that the destination MPLS node interprets are pushed onto the packet, such as the GAL. The TTL for these labels is set according to the standards that define them.

Second, the SFF Label is pushed to identify the desired SFF in the receiving MPLS node. The TTL for this MPLS label MUST be set to 1 to avoid mis-forwarding.

Third, zero or more additional labels are pushed such that the resulting label stack will cause the packet to be transported to the destination MPLS node, and such that when the packet arrives at that node either the SFF Label is at the top of the label stack, which is typically the case when penultimate hop popping is used at the penultimate node, or, as part of normal MPLS processing, the SFF Label becomes the top label in the stack before the packet is forwarded to another node and before the packet is dispatched to a higher layer. The TTL for these labels is set by configuration or to the defaults for normal MPLS operation in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending node pushes three groups of labels onto the packet. Labels the far end interprets itself go on first. Then comes the SFF Label, whose time-to-live is set to 1 so that a packet that somehow loops cannot be forwarded wrongly. Finally the ordinary transport labels go on, arranged so that the SFF Label is at the top of the stack by the time the packet is handed up at the far end.

sections.title: Processing at the Destination Node
sections.content:
The destination MPLS node performs a lookup on the SFF Label to retrieve the next-hop context between the SFF and the service function, for example the destination Media Access Control address in the case where native Ethernet encapsulation is used between the SFF and the service function. How the next-hop context is populated is out of scope for this document.

The receiving SFF SHOULD check that the received SFF Label has a TTL of 1 upon receipt. Any other value indicates a likely error condition and SHOULD result in discarding the packet. The receiving MPLS node then pops the SFF Label, and any labels beneath it, so that the destination SFF receives the SFC packet with the NSH at the top of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: At the far end, the label is looked up to find where the service function sits, the label and anything under it are removed, and the packet is handed to the forwarding instance with the Network Service Header now on top.

sections.title: Equal-Cost Multipath and Operations
sections.content:
There are equal-cost multipath (ECMP) considerations for payloads carried by MPLS. Many existing routers use deep packet inspection to examine the payload of an MPLS packet. If the first nibble of the payload is equal to 0x4 or 0x6, these routers, sometimes incorrectly, assume that the payload is IPv4 or IPv6 respectively, and as a result perform ECMP load balancing based on presumed information present in IP, TCP or UDP payload headers, or in a combination of the MPLS label stack and presumed IP, TCP or UDP payload headers.

For SFC, ECMP may or may not be desirable. To prevent ECMP when it is not desired, the NSH Base Header was carefully constructed so that the NSH could not look like IPv4 or IPv6 based on its first nibble. The default behavior for MPLS-encapsulated SFC is therefore not to use ECMP other than by using entropy derived from the MPLS label stack, which results in all packets going to the same service function taking the same path regardless of the use of ECMP in the network.

If ECMP is desired when SFC is used with an MPLS transport network, there are two possible options: entropy labels, and flow-aware transport labels. A recommendation on choosing between these options, and on their proper placement in the label stack, is left for future study.

On operations, administration and maintenance, OAM at the SFC layer is handled by SFC-defined mechanisms. However, OAM may be required at the MPLS transport layer, in which case standard MPLS-layer OAM mechanisms such as the GAL may be used at the transport label layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers look at the first nibble of the payload to guess whether it is IPv4 or IPv6, and use that guess to spread traffic over several equal-cost paths. The Network Service Header was built so that it cannot be mistaken for either, so by default all the packets going to one service function follow the same path. If a network does want that spreading, the RFC names two ways to get it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document describes a method for transporting SFC packets using the NSH over an MPLS transport network. It follows well-established MPLS procedures in widespread operational use. It does not define any new protocol elements or allocate any new code points, and it is no more or less secure than carrying any other protocol over MPLS. To the MPLS network, the NSH and its contents are simply an opaque payload. The security considerations of RFC 8595 also apply to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is exposed by this scheme. It reuses ordinary MPLS labelling, allocates no new code points, and the MPLS network treats the Network Service Header and everything inside it as an opaque payload, exactly as it would treat any other traffic.
